---
title: "Size and drawing of equations"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  dev = "ragg_png",
  dpi = 150
)
```

```{r setup}
library(equatags)
library(grid)
```

'equatags' lays out equations itself, with the rules of TeX and the
parameters of the 'MATH' table of an OpenType math font. It does not need a
graphic device, a browser or Word:

- `equation_size()` gives the width, the height above the baseline and the
  depth below it;
- `equation_grob()` draws the equation with 'grid' (R >= 4.3), with the
  glyphs of the font.

The default font is 'STIX Two Math', shipped with 'gdtools': the results
only depend on this file, they are the same on every machine.

## Size of equations

```{r}
eqs <- c(
  "\\frac{a+b}{c}",
  "\\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2",
  "\\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}",
  "\\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\\\ c & d \\end{pmatrix}"
)
equation_size(eqs, size = 12)
```

Sizes are in inches, at the font size `size` in points. Multiplied by 72,
they are in points:

```{r}
round(equation_size(eqs, size = 12) * 72, 1)
```

The display style (`display = TRUE`, as `$$...$$`) is larger: fractions,
and the limits of sums above and below the operator.

```{r}
rbind(
  inline = equation_size("\\sum_{i=1}^{n} \\frac{x_i}{n}"),
  display = equation_size("\\sum_{i=1}^{n} \\frac{x_i}{n}", display = TRUE)
)
```

An equation that 'KaTeX' can not read gives `NA` with a warning.

Another math font can be used with `font`: the path of a font file, or a
family name found by 'systemfonts', such as `"Latin Modern Math"`,
`"Libertinus Math"` or `"Cambria Math"`.

## Drawing

`equation_grob()` returns a grob placed at `x0`, `y0` (in `"npc"` units by
default) and justified with `hjust` and `vjust`; `colour` sets its colour.

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 1.2}
grid.newpage()
grid.draw(
  equation_grob(
    "f(x) = \\frac{1}{\\sigma\\sqrt{2\\pi}} e^{-\\frac{(x-\\mu)^2}{2\\sigma^2}}",
    size = 16, display = TRUE
  )
)
```

Its size is known without drawing it: `grobWidth()`, `grobHeight()`,
`grobAscent()` and `grobDescent()` give the size of the equation and the
parts above and below the baseline. To place the baseline of an equation at
`y0`, for example on the baseline of a text, justify it vertically by the
share of its depth in its height:

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 1}
tex <- "\\bar{x} = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i"
s <- equation_size(tex, size = 14)
eq <- equation_grob(
  tex, size = 14, x0 = 0.55, y0 = 0.4,
  hjust = 0, vjust = s$depth / (s$height + s$depth),
  colour = "#C0392B"
)
grid.newpage()
grid.text("The mean is ", x = 0.55, y = 0.4, just = c(1, 0), gp = gpar(fontsize = 14))
grid.draw(eq)
grid.lines(y = c(0.4, 0.4), gp = gpar(col = "grey70", lty = 2))
```

## In a ggplot2 graphic

An equation grob can be added to a 'ggplot2' graphic with
`annotation_custom()`:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
library(ggplot2)

eq <- equation_grob(
  "\\hat{y} = \\beta_0 + \\beta_1 x",
  size = 14, x0 = 0.95, y0 = 0.95, hjust = 1, vjust = 1
)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  annotation_custom(eq) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The package 'munch' draws equations written as `$...$` in markdown texts:
titles, labels and annotations of 'ggplot2' graphics.

## With flextable

'flextable' uses `equation_size()` for the width of the columns that
contain equations (`autofit()`, `dim_pretty()`) and `equation_grob()` to
draw them in images (`gen_grob()`, `save_as_image()`):

```{r, fig.width = 4, fig.height = 1.4}
library(flextable)

ft <- flextable(data.frame(
  formula = c("e^{i\\pi} + 1 = 0", "\\int_0^1 x^2 \\, dx = \\frac{1}{3}")
))
ft <- mk_par(ft, j = "formula", value = as_paragraph(as_equation(formula)))
ft <- autofit(ft)
plot(ft)
```

## Differences with Word

The layout follows the rules of TeX, as LaTeX and 'KaTeX' do. Compared with
Word displaying the same equation with the same font, widths differ by about
1% on usual equations. The known differences (spaces around binary
operators, matrices in parentheses...) are listed in the section
"Differences with Word and browsers" of `?equation_size`. Most of them make
the computed size a little larger than in Word, which is safe to size a cell
or a column.
